q: Why do we experience déjà vu?
Why do we have déjà vu?
Why do we feel like we've been somewhere before?
What is the science behind déjà vu?
a: Déjà vu is a common psychological phenomenon where a person feels as though they have already experienced a situation they are encountering for the first time. The most widely accepted explanation is the dual-processing theory, which suggests that déjà vu occurs when the brain's familiarity and recollection systems become momentarily out of sync. The familiarity system (in the perirhinal cortex) registers that a scene feels familiar, while the recollection system (in the hippocampus) fails to retrieve any actual memory of the experience, creating a sense of 'knowing without remembering.' Another theory, the memory overlap theory, proposes that déjà vu happens when a new experience closely resembles a forgotten past experience, triggering a false sense of familiarity. The attentional theory suggests that lapses in attention cause the brain to misinterpret a scene as familiar. Déjà vu affects 60-80% of people, most commonly those aged 15-25, and typically lasts only a few seconds. It is more common in people who are anxious, open to new experiences, or have better memory recall. Some people never experience déjà vu, possibly due to differences in how their brains process familiarity and novelty.

q: What are the theories of déjà vu?
a: Déjà vu, meaning 'already seen' in French, is the phenomenon of feeling like one has lived through the present situation before. It affects 60-80% of people, most commonly those aged 15-25. The main theories include the dual-processing theory (a mismatch between familiarity and recollection), the memory overlap theory (new experiences triggering memories of similar past events), and the attentional theory (lapses in attention causing the brain to misinterpret a scene as familiar).
